statements: The chief concern is a slowly progressive neurologic syndrome localized to the lumbosacral spine.
The neurologic syndrome includes worsening left greater than right lower-extremity weakness and numbness over several years.
The neurologic syndrome includes chronic low back pain.
The neurologic syndrome includes constipation.
These symptoms suggest a chronic compressive or infiltrative lesion affecting the lumbar spinal canal or cauda equina region rather than an acute vascular or inflammatory process.
The patient has a prior history of a lumbar spinal tumor resected in 1992.
The lumbar spinal tumor was diagnosed at that time as paraganglioma.
The patient received radiation therapy in 2002.
Surveillance imaging showed interval enlargement of the lumbar lesion.
Current CT shows expansion of the spinal canal by an isodense soft-tissue mass.
Current CT shows osseous destruction.
MRI shows a mass that is hypointense on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences.
MRI shows homogeneous postcontrast enhancement.
There is focal sensory loss in the left groin, anterior thigh, and calf.
There is bilateral leg weakness.
The bilateral leg weakness is worse on the left.
The focal sensory loss and bilateral leg weakness support mass effect on lumbar nerve roots or conus/cauda equina structures.
Constipation supports chronic neural compromise.
There is no mention of acute onset.
There is no mention of fever.
There is no mention of systemic infection.
There is no mention of inflammatory symptoms.
The course is over years.
The course over years argues strongly against acute disc herniation or hematoma.
The patient has a history of prostate cancer.
The lesion appears to be a long-standing recurrent lumbar canal mass at the site of a previously resected tumor.
The lesion appears to be a long-standing recurrent lumbar canal mass at the site of a previously resected tumor, making a new metastatic lesion less likely.
The MRI pattern is not typical for many common intradural tumors such as myxopapillary ependymoma.
Myxopapillary ependymoma more often shows T2 hyperintensity rather than marked T2 hypointensity.
The combination of osseous destruction and very delayed recurrence after prior surgery and radiation raises concern that the original diagnosis may have been incorrect.
Recurrent spinal paraganglioma fits the prior diagnosis.
Recurrent spinal paraganglioma fits the location in the lumbar canal.
Recurrent spinal paraganglioma fits homogeneous enhancement.
Recurrent spinal paraganglioma fits slow progression over years.
Spinal paragangliomas are typically highly vascular.
Spinal paragangliomas are often T2 hyperintense or show a salt-and-pepper appearance rather than uniformly T2 hypointense.
Osseous destruction is less characteristic of spinal paraganglioma.
Cellular schwannoma of the lumbar spine can present as a slow-growing cauda equina or lumbar canal mass causing chronic radiculopathy, weakness, sensory loss, and bowel dysfunction.
Cellular schwannomas can erode adjacent bone.
Cellular schwannomas may be mistaken histologically for other spindle-cell or neuroendocrine tumors, especially in older pathology.
MRI often shows iso- to hypointensity on T1-weighted sequences in cellular schwannoma.
MRI often shows relatively low T2 signal compared with conventional schwannoma because of hypercellularity in cellular schwannoma.
MRI often shows homogeneous enhancement in cellular schwannoma.
The history of a lesion originally called paraganglioma but recurring locally over decades with these imaging features strongly supports cellular schwannoma.
Prostate cancer can cause back pain, weakness, and osseous involvement.
This lesion is centered in the spinal canal at the site of a previously resected tumor.
This lesion has a decades-long local recurrence pattern rather than typical multifocal vertebral metastatic disease.
The location and chronic symptoms fit myxopapillary ependymoma or another cauda equina tumor.
The imaging description of T2 hypointensity and osseous destruction is less typical for myxopapillary ependymoma or another cauda equina tumor.
The most compelling synthesis is a recurrent cellular schwannoma of the lumbar spine.
The lesion was previously labeled paraganglioma.
The very slow indolent course is a decisive clue.
The lesion is a recurrent lumbar canal mass causing chronic cauda equina-type deficits.
CT evidence of spinal canal expansion with osseous destruction is a decisive clue.
MRI showing T1 and T2 hypointensity with homogeneous enhancement is a decisive clue.
These features are characteristic of a hypercellular schwannoma.
These features are less typical for paraganglioma or metastatic disease.
The differential diagnosis includes cellular schwannoma of the lumbar spine.
The differential diagnosis includes recurrent spinal paraganglioma.
The differential diagnosis includes metastatic prostate cancer to the lumbar spine.
The differential diagnosis includes myxopapillary ependymoma.
The final diagnosis is cellular schwannoma.
